$ETH is missing something to really pump:

Ethereum needs to connect the institutional adoption story with $ETH the asset to really BOOM.

Right now the dominant narrative is commoditization of infra: blockspace and DA are becoming abundant and cheap.

So adoption grows but the burn doesn't grow with it. 

And as adoption increases, ETH as gas gets abstracted away too.

I believe the strongest story is ETH becoming a security asset for institutions around the world.

If assets are not just wrappers of tradfi assets but NATIVELY issued on Ethereum, Ethereum's security becomes a national security issue.

Countries and financial giants wouldn't trust retail stakers or a few dominant LSTs like Lido to secure trillions in assets. 

They'd want to stake and process txs themselves. 

Perhaps even sanctioned countries would stake just to not be excluded from blockspace.

And this doesn't strictly need native issuance, because at some scale of RWAs a reorg or an attack already becomes too expensive to leave to someone else.

The burn ties ETH demand to fees, which are collapsing.

Staking ties ETH demand to the value being secured, which is growing!!!

Native issuance of assets plus ETH as a necessity asset for institutional staking is the sexy story that could pump ETH to $100k.

High inflation can age very differently.

@Aptos and @SuiNetwork are good examples.

Their yearly inflation since TGE looked almost identical at first, then diverged sharply:

→ $APT: 183.28% → 147.55% → 45.80%
→ $SUI: 189.29% → 26.32% → 10.33%

For holders, that difference is important because higher inflation means more new supply competing with existing tokens.

If demand doesn’t grow fast enough to absorb it, that creates more dilution and potentially more sell pressure.

A big reason is the supply schedule. Aptos kept heavier investor/contributor unlocks, while Sui’s emissions fell much faster.

Aptos is reducing that pressure now too, with lower staking rewards and its initial investor/contributor unlock cycle ending in October.

Right now, SUI has a lot less new supply to absorb.

Strictly looking at supply pressure, buying SUI makes more sense.

Bitcoin is finally entering a new phase.

It started as digital P2P money, evolved into digital gold, then moved onto corporate balance sheets and into ETFs.

Now, the market is building a deeper financial layer around $BTC.

Let's analyze this BTC expansion over the years ↓

1/ $BTC as Money

Bitcoin’s first use case was straightforward: money that could move directly between two people without a bank in the middle.

For the early Bitcoin crowd, this was revolutionary.

→ Payments
→ Self-custody
→ Moving value across borders

Together, they made Bitcoin useful as money without relying on traditional financial rails.

But as adoption grew, the narrative expanded beyond payments.

Bitcoin’s fixed supply and rising value led more people to treat it as a long-term asset.

That’s when the “digital gold” thesis really started taking shape.

2/ $BTC as an Institutional Asset

The “digital gold” thesis gradually moved beyond crypto-native investors.

@Strategy started adding BTC to its corporate treasury in 2020.

Then other public companies followed:

→ Block
→ Tesla
→ Metaplanet

Corporate adoption was only one part of the shift.

In 2024, spot Bitcoin ETFs launched in the U.S., giving traditional investors a much easier way to gain exposure.

Btw, U.S. spot ETFs and public companies now hold roughly 2.5M BTC combined.

By then, Bitcoin had become a serious asset for both corporate treasuries and traditional investors.

That scale created a much bigger market for financial products built around BTC.

3/ $BTC as Productive Capital

IMO, this is the most important phase.

BTC is now getting the same kind of financial layer ETH has had for years, with staking, lending, liquid tokens, and eventually strategies like looping.

I talked about this recently when I broke down how stBTC could make looping possible on Bitcoin.

And @Stacks is pushing this further with Bitcoin Staking.

Under the initial design, every $100 of BTC bonded needs roughly $5 worth of $STX locked alongside it.

So more BTC entering = more STX being committed alongside it.

And STX already has a history of amplifying Bitcoin moves.

I checked five major BTC rallies across different cycles:

→ STX outperformed in 4 of 5
→ Median STX upside was ~3.3x BTC’s return

The recent move fits that pattern again, with STX up ~116% over the past 7 days.

A good reminder of why I call it BTC beta.

Conclusion

I’ve always liked STX as a higher-beta Bitcoin bet. Now there’s finally more utility underneath that relationship.

If Bitcoin keeps evolving into a more productive asset, I think STX has a much better reason to stay attached to that growth than it did in previous cycles.

Disclosure: I’m a long-time $STX holder and Stacks supporter.

Actually, a pretty insane pump and one of BTC’s quickest moves in a while.

I’m still bullish on the bigger picture, but I wouldn’t be shocked to see a cooldown before any real continuation.

This is a good start, but I’d rather see it consolidate than just keep chasing a straight line up. Stay safe.

Could Avalanche give community banks access to institutional capital?

Loan securitization is prohibitively expensive for many community banks. Deals often need to exceed $500 million to be economically viable, leaving smaller loan portfolios without a practical route to capital markets.

Intain’s securitization platform on Avalanche has already onboarded more than $38B in cumulative deal value across 325k+ loans. Intain and FIS have launched the Digital Liquidity Gateway, which runs on a dedicated Avalanche L1 and integrates directly with FIS banking systems.

The gateway tokenizes each loan individually so loan data and ownership can be verified onchain without manual reconciliation. It is designed to lower the cost of securitization enough to make deals below $100 million viable for the first time.

This model could give community banks access to institutional capital if it works at scale.

🌎 Globalization is often discussed through the lens of tariffs and trade wars but the latest OECD data points that global competition is increasingly between companies backed by states.

📊 In 2024, subsidies received by the large industrial firms tracked by the OECD reached $108 billion (1.3% of revenue), the highest relative level since the global financial crisis. Back on 2029, the ratio spiked largely because of emergency support for Western automakers and collapsing revenues during the crisis. Today, the increase is more structural as governments are once again directly supporting strategic industries such as semiconductors, solar and steel. 1.3% of revenue may sound small but for a company operating at a 5% margin this would represent more than a quarter of operating profit which is enough to completely reshape the economics of an industry.

🇨🇳 China is where the phenomenon is most pronounced as the Chinese firms received three to eight times more public support than competitors in developed economies. Moreover, around 60% of the relative market-share gains achieved by Chinese firms can be associated with subsidy intensity versus roughly 22% for all firms that gained market share.

📈 These subsidies appear to increase market share without significantly improving productivity or profitability. Their purpose is not necessarily to create the most profitable companies today but to allow firms to invest more, maintain excess capacity, tolerate lower prices and accept returns on capital that private competitors could not sustain for as long. Typical of what we are seeing in solar for example.

⚠️ Now, this is no longer just a Chinese story as the US, Europe, Japan and South Korea have all relaunched industrial policies. The current trade war is in fact becoming a balance-sheet war between governments. Therefore, for investors the implication is important because we can no longer analyse some industries using only traditional concepts such as margins, ROIC and financial discipline. If a competitor can tolerate ten years of poor returns because its government sees the industry as strategically important, its own economics become much more fragile.

In that environment, understanding who finances an industry at what cost and for what strategic purpose becomes almost as important as understanding the company itself.

*OECD link: https://t.co/4uizkSMYFL

I think, even for ordinary users, there should be two degrees of freedom available when you define the effort spent on a prompt. 
- power/parallelism (width) and
- deliberation time (depth)

the total effort is the product of the two, or the area of the rectangle.

there are different approaches to compute that satisfy different user needs: 

- bursty/wide+shallow: "I'm ok with spending a lot of tokens, and I need an answer now"
- deep/narrow+long: "I care more about answer quality and i'm willing to trade away some latency" 
- maximal/wide+deep: "throw everything at it for a while"

bursty reasoning is the kind I find myself wanting the most. I'm willing to trade off token budget for latency. right now if you dial effort to max you get a long query (timewise), more like wide and deep. 

I would bet a lot of users feel the same way.

Most VCs prefer serial entrepreneurs.

I don't.

I back first-time entrepreneurs more than most.

Yes, it's riskier, but the returns can be much bigger.

Second-time entrepreneurs are usually better operationally. They make sure they raise the RIGHT amount of money. They're ruthless about hiring.

But first-time entrepreneurs? They tend to raise too much money. They feel like they have to hire everybody. Then they hit the wall and wonder why the next round didn't come as easily.

Second-time entrepreneurs who've hit the wall know to keep it thin until product-market fit. Grow organically. Don't rely on the venture capital marketplace because it comes and goes.

I like first-time entrepreneurs making this their career. This might be the one they were meant to be.

I like second-time entrepreneurs going after something entirely different. Not recreating their old business.

Bill Gates, Steve Jobs, Mark Zuckerberg, Larry Ellison… first-time entrepreneurs.

Reserve Bank of Kansas City (sponsor of Jackson Hole) titled this year's theme as "Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy."

So ignorant media hosts like Dani Burger said it would be sooo disappointing if Warsh talks about Stablecoins?

Wrong!

Here's why...

3 key points that need to be wrapped together to understand the future of the global monetary system:

1) Increased Treasury buybacks are just the beginning of a more activist Bessent. Prior to his appointment as SecTres, he stated prominently that he wanted to be a part of the remaking the global financial order in a way that has not been done since Bretton Woods. He's beginning to act on that desire. 

2) Warsh talked more about reducing the balance sheet prior to his appointment than about hiking rates. At the time, many saw this as negative for the debasement trade: gold, BTC, etc. How wrong those thoughts are.

3) Warsh is expected to spend at least some time tomorrow am on stablecoins. Many think that topic doesn't relate to rising rates and the fiscal situation. Once again, how wrong those thoughts are.

Putting this all together:

The debt and specifically the net interest expense have gotten out of control. US must bring down it's cost of borrowing. As I posted earlier this week, there is a simple way to do this. Buyback higher coupon notes/bonds and reissue bills (short-term debt).

But who will buy all these T-Bills? And how does that relate to the Fed's balance sheet as well as stablecoins?

There is a huge demand for Bills, but if the Treasury really wants to fund itself with Bills going forward, it will need much more demand. Enter the balance sheet and stablecoins.

Stablecoins buy bills: That is an easy one. But seeing the connection to the Fed balance sheet is trickier, but not really.

Very simply, it's called a balance sheet b/c assets (+SH equity) must equal liabilities.

What are the Fed's assets? Mortgages and Treasuries mostly.

What are the Fed's liabilities? Mostly bank reserves and some paper bills.

Thus, if Warsh wants to reduce the Fed balance sheet, he can't simply start selling (or stop rolling) over current assets. Assets must equate to liabilities. This is why Powell restarted QE earlier this year with a Bill buying program. So that banks could keep more reserves with the Fed. 

Thus, Warsh must also significantly reduce liabilities should he wish to reduce assets. In other words, he must force banks to lower reserves.

So, and this is a bit complicated, but I will boil it down here. Warsh will need to force banks out of reserves. The closest monetary cousin to reserves, is, you guessed it, T-Bills.

Thus, a massive shortening of Treasury duration is underway, shifting even more the $40T in debt to the short end. But there must be buyers: The banks and stablecoins.

Warsh speaking on stablecoins tomorrow is not some unrelated topic to the major issues of today. It is the topic.
